platforms.title: Hyperthyroidism or Anxiety? The Heart Rate Clue
platforms.meta_description: Racing heart and constant nervousness can look like anxiety, but a resting pulse over 100 and weight loss despite eating more point somewhere else.
platforms.body_html:
A racing heart, constant nervousness, and trouble sleeping — these look exactly like anxiety, and case reports describe hyperthyroidism being misdiagnosed as an anxiety disorder for exactly this reason. Both conditions share the same core symptoms because both involve the nervous system running in overdrive. But two specific details tend to separate them, and neither one is something anxiety alone typically causes.

The Resting Heart Rate Test

According to clinical sources, a resting heart rate consistently above 100 beats per minute — measured after sitting calmly, not right after stress or exercise — is a red flag for a thyroid problem rather than anxiety alone. Anxiety can speed up the heart temporarily during a stressful moment, but a pulse that stays elevated even first thing in the morning, right after waking up calm, points toward the thyroid pumping out too much hormone around the clock.

Losing Weight While Eating More

The other detail is weight change. Clinical sources describe hyperthyroidism's classic pattern as weight loss with a normal or increased appetite — eating the same or more, and still losing weight, because the excess thyroid hormone accelerates metabolism. Anxiety alone doesn't reliably cause this combination; appetite changes with anxiety usually go the other way, or weight stays roughly stable.

Other Details Worth Noting

Heat intolerance (feeling too warm when others feel fine), hand tremor, and heavy sweating round out the picture — none of these are required for a diagnosis, but having several together strengthens the case for a thyroid cause over anxiety alone. In older adults, hyperthyroidism can look different again, sometimes showing up as fatigue, low mood, or confusion instead of the classic racing-heart picture — which makes it even easier to miss.

Why It's Worth Getting This Right

Treating hyperthyroidism as anxiety alone doesn't just delay the real fix — anti-anxiety medication doesn't address the excess thyroid hormone driving the racing heart, so symptoms tend to persist or worsen despite treatment, and the constant strain on the heart from a chronically elevated pulse is itself a reason not to let this go unchecked for months. That's a different risk profile from ordinary anxiety, which doesn't carry the same cardiovascular load over time.

What to Actually Do

The diagnosis itself is simple: a blood test measuring TSH and thyroid hormone levels, not a guessing game based on symptoms alone. If anxiety-like symptoms come with a resting pulse over 100 or unexplained weight loss despite a normal appetite, that combination is worth mentioning specifically when booking a doctor's visit — it points the workup toward the thyroid from the start instead of starting with an anxiety diagnosis alone, and can save weeks of trial-and-error with treatments aimed at the wrong cause.

Next time your heart races for no clear reason, take a moment to check your resting pulse while sitting calmly, ideally more than once over a few days — a number that consistently reads over 100 is worth mentioning to a doctor alongside how your weight and appetite have been trending recently.
